title: Chapter IX
focus: the funeral and the meaning of the dream

teacherSummary.text: Almost no one comes to Gatsby's funeral; his father, Henry Gatz, arrives with a boyhood schedule of self-improvement. Wolfshiem refuses to come. Nick ends things with Jordan, meets Tom, and decides to return West. He reflects on the green light and the American dream.

context.history: The funeral's emptiness contrasts with the crowds at the parties. Henry Gatz's pride in his son's wealth and the boyhood 'schedule' echo Benjamin Franklin's famous plan of self-improvement in his Autobiography, a founding text of the American self-made man.

significance: Nick moves from Gatsby's story to America's: the Dutch sailors' 'fresh, green breast of the new world' links Gatsby's longing to the nation's founding dream, and the last sentence makes the struggle against the past universal.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter IX,” how does Fitzgerald show the funeral and the meaning of the dream? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the structure you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter IX, how does Fitzgerald develop the idea of the funeral and the meaning of the dream? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the structure in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IX develops the idea of the funeral and the meaning of the dream. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter IX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its structure shape the reader's understanding of the funeral and the meaning of the dream. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter IX suggests about the funeral and the meaning of the dream. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's structure and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how F. Scott Fitzgerald uses structure in Chapter IX to complicate the reader's understanding of the funeral and the meaning of the dream. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the funeral and the meaning of the dream responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter IX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the funeral and the meaning of the dream follows or bends those conventions, using the structure as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter IX and its treatment of the funeral and the meaning of the dream. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's structure and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter IX as evidence for a larger claim about the funeral and the meaning of the dream in The Great Gatsby. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the funeral and the meaning of the dream. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Great Gatsby.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
